Speckled rockfish (Sebastes ovalis) attain a maximum total length of 56 centimeters [Li = 56 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper range reported for members of the subgenus Sebastomus, reflecting the species' slow growth and extended longevity in cold, deep-water habitats. Field surveys of older adult specimens collected off the central California coast have confirmed that this asymptotic length is a reliable indicator of full somatic maturity. The length-weight relationship, parameterized as the cube of total length multiplied by a constant, yields an estimated ultimate wet weight of approximately 2,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,500 grams] for individuals approaching this maximum size, based on extensive sampling across multiple age classes.

Sexual maturation in Sebastes ovalis is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age alone, with the onset of puberty estimated at a total length of 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters]. Individuals that cross this threshold typically exhibit the first macroscopic signs of gonadal development, including vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Individual fish generally attain the corresponding wet body mass of approximately 296.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 296.3 grams] at the onset of puberty, a value derived from the same regional length-weight relationship. This weight is typically reached during the third or fourth year of life under average coastal thermal regimes, although local variation in prey availability can shift this developmental timeline by several months. Puberty marks a critical life-history transition after which somatic growth and initial reproductive investment proceed concurrently.

Reproductive output in this viviparous species begins with the internal fertilization of oocytes following copulation during late summer. Gravid females give birth to fully developed larvae, each with a wet weight of approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams] at parturition. This minute larval mass, derived from the volume of a mature egg with a diameter of 0.8 millimeters, reflects the extreme energetic dilution typical of high-fecundity marine teleosts. The species is capable of producing an estimated 160,000 larvae annually [Ri = 160,000 larvae annually] when maintained at a stable temperature of 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C], with this high fecundity compensating for the substantial mortality encountered during the prolonged pelagic larval phase.

Longevity estimates for Sebastes ovalis indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 37 years [am = approximately 37 years] under the typical thermal conditions along the outer continental shelf at 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C]. This estimate is derived from otolith-based age validation of the oldest individuals captured in deep-water rockfish surveys. The extended lifespan is characteristic of the genus, in which several members exceed 50 years, and it is coupled with an iteroparous reproductive strategy that distributes spawning effort across many seasons. The combination of slow somatic growth, delayed maturity, and high adult survival aligns with a conservative life-history strategy that renders the species vulnerable to overexploitation.

The developmental trajectory following parturition is dominated by a pelagic larval phase lasting several months before the onset of metamorphosis and subsequent settlement into demersal habitat. Newly released larvae rapidly transition from endogenous yolk reserves to exogenous feeding on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton. The extremely low body mass of approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams] at parturition necessitates immediate access to dense patches of suitable prey, as starvation can occur within days if adequate food concentrations are not encountered. Once settled, juvenile fish grow steadily within rocky reef refugia, attaining approximately 28 centimeters [Lp = approximately 28 centimeters] total length at sexual maturity and ultimately approaching the asymptotic maximum of 56 centimeters [Li = 56 centimeters] under favorable environmental conditions.
